title: Setting up an armature
content:
An armature is the skeleton that will bend the character. In this part you'll add one, extrude its bones up the spine and out along one arm and one leg, parent and place them where the body would bend, and name them. Naming them with .L and .R lets Blender mirror the arm and leg to the other side with Symmetrize. You'll need the finished character mesh from the last part. The video uses Blender 2.90.

Build the spine

  1. Add an armature. 0:00 Press Shift A and choose Armature. It adds a single bone at the origin, hidden inside the mesh, so turn on X-ray to see it. Select the armature and press Tab for Edit Mode, where you build the skeleton.

  2. Extrude bones up the spine. 0:27 Select the tip of the bone and press E to extrude a new bone from it. Click the middle mouse button to lock it to an axis, or press Z to lock it to Z. Extrude again up to the base of the neck 0:40, and once more up into the head 0:46.

Add the arm

  1. Extrude a bone out to the elbow. 0:51 Select the joint at the base of the neck, press E and bring the new bone out to the elbow.

  2. Disconnect it from the neck. 0:57 In the Bone Properties, under Relations, turn off Connected. Now you can move the bone over and drag each end into place, so it starts at the shoulder instead of the neck 1:08.

  3. Extrude to the wrist and the hand. 1:18 Extrude a bone out to the wrist, then another to the end of the hand. Work on one side only: you'll mirror it later 1:26.

Add the leg

  1. Duplicate a bone for the leg. 1:31 Select a bone, press Shift D to duplicate it, and rotate it to point down the leg.

  2. Parent it to the root bone. 1:39 Select the leg bone, then Shift-click the root bone (the first bone, at the top of the armature's hierarchy), press Ctrl P and choose Keep Offset. A dotted line shows the relationship.

  3. Place the leg bones. 2:02 Move the bone's tip down to the knee, extrude to the heel, then in the side view extrude to the toe and pull the joint down to the heel 2:09. The knee doesn't bend from the back of the leg, so move the knee joint toward the front 2:19.

  4. Clean up and check the parenting. 2:30 If you've extruded extra bones by accident, select them and press X to delete them. Move the top bone to check the leg is still parented 2:37.

Refine the spine

  1. Put the joints where the body bends. 2:43 Make sure the pelvis rotates from the right spot, and give the spine a slight curve. If a bone you deleted broke the leg's parenting, parent it again with Keep Offset 3:07.

  2. Disconnect the head bone. 3:19 Turn off Connected for the head bone too, move it up and scale it down a little. It controls the head's rotation, so move its base to the base of the head; the spine bone below runs up the back to the base of the neck 3:45.

  3. Line up the arm from above. 4:02 In the top view, move the elbow joint into place, then the wrist, lined up with the hand. Pull the shoulder up slightly if it needs it 4:11.

Name and mirror the bones

  1. Name every bone. 4:29 Select each bone and type its name in the name field at the top of the Bone Properties. The video uses pelvis (the root bone), lowerback, upperback, shoulder, forearm, hand, head, upperleg, lowerleg and foot 5:10.

  2. Add .L to the side's names. 5:10 To mirror bones, you select them and choose Armature → Symmetrize, but that only works with the right names 5:40. Select the arm bones and choose Armature → Names → AutoName Left/Right: it adds .L to their names, because Symmetrize will make the matching .R bones. Do the same for the leg and foot bones 5:56.

  3. Symmetrize. 6:06 Select all the arm and leg bones and choose Armature → Symmetrize. Now you have a full skeleton, fully named. Expand the armature in the Outliner to see how all the bones are parented 6:18.

  4. Show the names in the viewport. 6:28 In the Armature Properties, under Viewport Display, turn on Names to see each bone's name in the viewport. Axes shows how each bone is rotated 6:39: some point in different directions, which may need dealing with later. Turn it off again.

The video uses Blender 2.90. In Blender 4.0 and later, bone layers and bone groups were replaced by bone collections, so the grids of layer buttons in the Bone and Armature Properties, and the menu's Change Armature Layers and Change Bone Layers, aren't there any more. Nothing in this part uses them.

Wrap-up

The character now has a full skeleton: a curved spine from the pelvis to the head, and arms and legs on both sides, each bone named with .L or .R and parented so the chain moves together. Next you'll bind the mesh to it.
